study.title: Ezekiel 25 The Lord judges the neighboring nations that mocked Judah
study.overview: Ezekiel 25 gathers four oracles of judgment against the peoples near to Israel: Ammonites, Moabites, Edomites, and Philistines. The common point is not only political rivalry, but the arrogant reaction of these peoples to the fall of Jerusalem. They did not become neutral; they rejoiced, they despised the disgrace of Judah, and in some cases they actively acted against it. The chapter shows that the Lord judges not only his own people, but also the nations around, charging them for how they treated the covenant, the holy city, and the people of Judah. The repeated chorus will "know that I am the Lord" reveals that the purpose of judgment is to make the sovereignty of God visible.

outline.title: Judgment against Amom
outline.explanation: The prophet is sent against the Ammonites because they rejoiced with the profanation of the sanctuary, the desolation of the land of Israel, and the captivity of Judah. Therefore, the Lord promises to deliver Ammon to Eastern peoples, turn his land into pasture, and eliminate his strength among the nations.

outline.title: Judgment against Moab
outline.explanation: Moab and Seir despised Judah as if it were just another common nation. In response, God will open Moab's border for foreign invasion and possession, removing his security and his memory among the peoples.

outline.title: Judgment against Edom
outline.explanation: Edom is accused of revenge against the house of Judah; here the text highlights aggravated guilt for deliberate action. The Lord promises devastation on the land of Edom and declares that divine vengeance will be manifested through his people.

outline.title: Judgment against the Philistines
outline.explanation: The Philistines acted with ancient hostility and a desire for revenge against Judah. God responds with extended hand, exterminating the rest of the coast of the sea and executing great vengeance, so that they may recognize who He is.

study.context: The chapter is set in a series of oracles against neighboring nations, following the announcement of the fall of Jerusalem. The notes provided show that these prophecies came against people who mocked the calamity of Judah and, in some cases, participated in it. It is also observed that these statements show that the Lord rules not only Israel, but all nations, and that no one escapes his judgment by using the fall of Judah as a cause of triumph.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter affirms the universal sovereignty of God and his retributive justice. He is not indifferent to the pride of the nations, nor to the mockery against his people in times of suffering. Sin here is not only military or political; it is moral and spiritual: to despise what God has sanctified, to rejoice in the ruin of the other and to feed revenge. The final chorus of each bloc indicates that the knowledge of God can come both by his mercy and his judgment. It also appears that God can use one nation to discipline another, but that does not inocense anyone before him. In evangelical reading, the chapter points to the holiness of God, human responsibility and the need not to rejoice in the fall of others, but to fear the Lord.

scholarViews.insight: The Ammonites rejoiced at the fall of Judah and the profanation of the temple; therefore they would suffer invasion, destruction, and know that the Lord is the true God.
The Moabites were condemned for triumphing over the fall of Jerusalem and for treating Judah as if it were just another common nation.
The prophecy against the Philistines is presented as God's judgment because of their enmity against the Jews; the chapter is linked to historical fulfillment through Nebuchadnezzar.

questions: What does how I react to when I see the suffering of someone I don't like or with whom I disagree?
In what situations can I be treating the work of God as something common, how did the peoples who despised Judah?
How can I resist vengeance and mockery, trusting that the Lord sees and judges with righteousness?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to abandon any pleasure in the fall of the other, especially when the other is in distress. In practice, this means watching the speech, not celebrating other people's defeats, intercedeing rather than mocking and remembering that God is the judge of the nations and also of my own heart. A concrete application is to examine how we react to news of crisis involving people or groups that we don't like: instead of irony or approval, we must respond with fear of God, compassion and prayer.
study.uncertainty: The biblical text and the given notes do not inform all historical details of compliance directly; therefore, any mention of subsequent fulfillment must remain cautious and bound only to what the notes say. It is also not possible to state more than the notes allow on the exact extension of the "nations of the East" or on the complete chronology of events without resorting to external sources.
